introduction: Compress JPG, JPEG, PNG and still WebP images in your browser. Keep the original display dimensions, choose a quality mode or maximum-byte target, and compare the actual output before downloading.

sections.heading: What Is an Image Compressor?
sections.body:
An image compressor is a tool that reduces an image's file size by changing how its data is stored. Depending on the image format and selected method, it may remove unnecessary information, adjust image quality or reduce the number of colors.

The purpose is to create a file that is easier to upload, download, store or display online. FileCompresser supports several common image formats, each with different characteristics.

sections.heading: JPG and JPEG Images
sections.body: JPG and JPEG are widely used for photographs. They are suitable for product pictures, personal photographs, travel images and many website graphics. The compression process uses quality settings to balance file size and visible detail. Lower quality settings can produce smaller files, but they may also create visible artifacts around edges, textures and small text.

sections.heading: PNG Images
sections.body: PNG is commonly used for logos, screenshots, diagrams and graphics that need transparent backgrounds. Unlike JPG, PNG can preserve transparency. FileCompresser provides separate PNG modes, including Lossless, Smart, Maximum and Target size. The selected mode determines whether decoded pixels are preserved or colors may be reduced to create a smaller file.

sections.heading: WebP Images
sections.body: WebP is an image format designed for web use. It supports lossy and lossless compression, as well as transparency. It can be useful for website photographs and graphics where smaller downloads are important. However, an existing WebP image may already be optimized, so further compression does not always create a smaller result.

sections.heading: How to Compress Images Online
sections.body:
You can use FileCompresser without installing an image editing application.

1. Select JPG, JPEG, PNG or WebP images from your device.
2. Wait for the website to validate the selected files.
3. Open Settings to choose a compression mode or output format.
4. Start processing.
5. Compare the original and final image sizes.
6. Inspect the image quality and download the result.

Original image dimensions are preserved.

sections.heading: Choose the Right Compression Mode
sections.body: Selecting the right quality mode is important because different images have different requirements.

sections.heading: Maximum
sections.body: Maximum is an optional stronger compression mode. It applies a greater quality trade-off to reduce file size. For JPEG and WebP, this can affect visible image detail.

sections.heading: Balanced
sections.body: Balanced is the default for JPEG and WebP. It offers a more moderate approach when you want to reduce file size without choosing the strongest compression setting.

sections.heading: High Quality
sections.body: High Quality prioritizes more visual detail. The output may be larger than a result created with a stronger compression setting.

sections.heading: PNG Lossless
sections.body: PNG starts in Lossless mode, which preserves decoded image pixels and transparency. Choose Smart, Maximum or Target size explicitly when color reduction is acceptable.

sections.heading: Target Size
sections.body: Target Size attempts to create an image within a specified maximum file size. It checks the actual output bytes rather than simply estimating the result. If the requested size cannot be achieved, the tool reports that the target was not met.

sections.heading: Why Should You Compress Images for Websites?
sections.body:
Large images are one of the common reasons web pages contain heavy resources. When a website uses unnecessarily large photographs, visitors may need to download more data than required for the displayed image. Optimizing images can help reduce page weight and make website resources easier to load.

For website owners, image compression is useful for:

- Product photographs on online stores.
- Featured images in blog articles.
- Homepage banners and promotional graphics.
- Team photographs and business profiles.
- Screenshots and tutorial images.
- Portfolio and project galleries.

Image compression is only one part of website optimization. Dimensions, responsive image delivery, caching and other page resources also affect loading performance.

sections.heading: Are Image Dimensions Preserved?
sections.body:
Image compression changes how image information is encoded while preserving the displayed pixel dimensions. FileCompresser does not offer image resizing.

If your website needs a different image width or height, prepare those dimensions in an image editor before compression. Keep the full-size original for printing and future editing.

sections.heading: Do Compressed Images Lose Quality?
sections.body:
The answer depends on the selected format and compression method. JPEG and WebP lossy encoding can change image pixels. The difference may be difficult to notice at moderate settings, but stronger compression can affect fine details, gradients and text.

PNG Lossless preserves decoded pixels, while other PNG modes may reduce colors. Transparency can be preserved even when color information changes. Before replacing an original, compare both versions at the same display scale. Pay attention to small lettering, sharp edges, product details and transparent areas.

sections.heading: Private Image Processing in Your Browser
sections.body: Selected images are processed in your browser rather than uploaded to a compression server. Each image can be up to 50 MiB and 32 megapixels. Queues allow up to 500 files and 300 MiB in total. Browser memory can still limit processing below these bounds. Keep a source copy before trying a new encoding.

sections.heading: Compress Images for Everyday Use
sections.body: Whether you manage an online store, publish blog articles or simply need smaller photographs for sharing, image compression can make file management easier. FileCompresser gives you format-specific options for JPG, JPEG, PNG and WebP images. Select your files, choose a suitable mode and compare the output before downloading.
